title: Ali in the house
hook: young Ali, Abu Talib's son, is raised in the Prophet's home

segments.voice: Yesterday: Zayd chose. Offered his father's home, he stayed, and was called a son. Your line was: he chose to stay.

A hard year comes to Mecca. Ibn Ishaq calls it a severe famine, and says it hit Quraysh badly. One house feels it hard: Abu Talib's. He's the uncle who took in an orphaned nephew years before and gave him a place at the table. Now Abu Talib has a big family and not enough to feed them. And the nephew, grown now and married to Khadijah, has an idea. Today: Ali in the house.
screen: `A HARD YEAR IN MECCA.` → `ABU TALIB'S HOUSE STRAINS.` → `THE NEPHEW HAS AN IDEA.`

segments.voice: Day seven hundred eleven gave this plan in a sentence. Here it is up close, as Ibn Ishaq tells it. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ goes to another uncle, al-Abbas: your brother Abu Talib has a large family, and you can see how hard things are. Let's lighten his load. I'll take one of his sons, you take one. Al-Abbas agrees, and they ask Abu Talib together. So two boys change houses that year. Al-Abbas takes Ja'far. The Prophet takes Ali, a small boy, into his home with Khadijah, where he joins Zayd, the boy who chose to stay. A household that keeps making room. Ibn Ishaq says Ali stayed with him from then on, and when revelation came, Ali followed him and believed. Later, the paths read Ali's place in more than one way. Sunni tradition counts him among the rightly guided caliphs; Shia tradition holds him to be the Imam after the Prophet. But here he is still a child at Khadijah's table. Ali wasn't an orphan; his father was alive. The man who took him in had been one, though. And in Sahih al-Bukhari, that man says the one who looks after an orphan will be with him in Paradise like this, holding up two fingers side by side. The house that raised Ali was run by someone who knew what that care was worth.
screen: `A PLAN TO LIGHTEN THE LOAD.` · `TWO BOYS CHANGE HOUSES.` · `A HOUSEHOLD THAT MAKES ROOM.` · `TWO FINGERS SIDE BY SIDE.` · then, large: `RAISED IN THAT HOUSE.`

segments.voice: Think of a child in your world who isn't yours, a niece, a neighbor's kid, a student, or of an adult who did that for you when you were small. Ask one plain question: what would lighten the load? A meal, a ride, an hour, a kind word to a tired parent; if you pray, pray for that child by name.
Ali. Abu Talib's young son, taken into the Prophet's own home with Khadijah in a hard year, and raised there. Today's word.
Your line: raised in that house. A home that kept making room. Seven hundred twenty days now.

screen: `DAY 720 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE BLACK STONE LIFTED TOGETHER.`

howItsDone: Muslims who sponsor or care for orphans often recall the Prophet's ﷺ words about the two fingers side by side, and Ali's upbringing in his home is told when Muslims remember Ali.

chat.meaning: Ibn Ishaq says that in a hard year the Prophet and al-Abbas each took a son of Abu Talib; the Prophet took Ali.

notes: Ibn Ishaq says Ali was the first male to believe; the script deliberately says only that he 'followed him and believed', to avoid a precedence claim that tomorrow's or later lessons may treat (and where Sunni sources also name Abu Bakr and Zayd). Keeper may decide to add it.
Ali's age is not given on purpose; reports differ.
Abu Talib's own request ('leave me Aqil') is omitted; confirm the paraphrase of the plan.
Sunni (a rightly guided caliph) and Shia (the Imam after the Prophet) descriptions of Ali stated side by side; confirm fair.
Sahih al-Bukhari 5304: confirm number and that kafil al-yatim is the wording behind 'looks after an orphan'.
Original: كَفَالَة (kafalah) is the noun; the hadith uses kafil. Confirm acceptable as the day's original word.

Fixed the hadith framing (it is about orphans, not 'a child who isn't yours'; Ali was not an orphan). Cut 'nobody calls it repayment', 'there for everything that came next' and 'both look back to this house'; Sunni/Shia lines now say 'tradition'. Replaced the repeated myth item.
